senses: A weekday on a Church calendar on which no feast is observed.
A furry pet considered a child by a human.
examples: Mrs. Jackson still kept doggie biscuits in her pockets, even though her furbaby had died two months ago.

As I took the satiny-furred cat into my arms, his purring ratcheted up a couple of notches. Brian stood looking at the two of us, grinning, then said of the malnourished creature, “I guess we have a furbaby!”
He looked down at the puppy fast asleep in his arms. Maybe this furbaby would slow down the ticking of her biological clock, too.

senses: Describing various weapons that use atmospheric oxygen to produce a blast wave of a significantly longer duration than those produced by condensed explosives.
ety: From thermo- + baric, derived from the Ancient Greek words for “heat” and “pressure”: θερμοβαρικός (thermobarikós), from θερμός (thermós, “hot”) + βάρος (báros, “weight, pressure”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”).
examples: Fears have risen over the use of thermobaric weapons by Russia after the Ukrainian ambassador to the US said a vacuum bomb – another term for the weapon – had been used during the invasion.
As he spoke, soldiers scrawled messages of retribution on the wings of a dozen drones, each packed with thermobaric explosives.

senses: Synonym of higgledy-piggledy.
examples: Small in scale, the town still reminded him of the ugly underside of cities he had seen from trains, of rubbish tumbling over rubbish along the embankments, higgledy houses, beaten streets.

Your view towards the Old Town is, for me, the most wonderful cityscape in the world — a pulsing crowd of higgledy houses, stacked, ready to topple, like spectators craning their necks to see into the New Town.
She thought about Montenello with its steep streets and higgledy houses, of summer sunshine, big bowls of pasta and glasses of flinty red wine.

senses: Having the character of a torch song.
A North American wildcat (Lynx rufus), having tufted ears and a short tail.
ety: From bob (short hair; with reference to its tail) + cat.

senses: One who follows or tails surreptitiously, as an investigator.
A large noose with a long handle intended to secure a fish's tail.
A fish bottom-feeding in shallow water with its tail out of the water.
examples: I had to concentrate on staying out of sight, yet close enough not to be stranded on the wrong side of a stoplight. I was working so hard at it that I didn't notice that the tailer had become the tailee.
When the car entered the traffic circle I followed after it, the tailed now tailing the tailer. The car's occupants, sure now that they'd been spotted, sped off ahead of me along Dodgers Hole Road.

senses: A truant; one who is absent without permission, especially from school.
ety: From skive (“play truant”) + -er. Probably from French esquiver (“slink away”).

senses: Used in normal daylight.
A devout Muslim.
ety: From Urdu نَمازی (namāzī), from Urdu نَماز (namāz) and their source, Persian نَمَاز.

senses: Consisting of or containing chalk.
Resembling chalk in some way.
examples: The dim, chalky lighting and unsteady camera movements.

senses: Able to secrete milk or a milky fluid such as latex.
examples: The sprouts proliferate and canalize to form the lactiferous ducts and the outbuddings form the alveoli of the mammary glands.

senses: An engraving tool, a stylus.
ety: From French stylet (“stiletto”), from Middle French stilet (“stiletto”), from Old Italian stiletto. Doublet of stiletto. By surface analysis, style + -et.

senses: An edible Asiatic pennywort (Centella asiatica)
such as edible dollarweed (Hydrocotyle umbellata).
Anemone hepatica.
Virginia pennywort (Obolaria virginica)
Ivy-leaved toadflax (Cymbalaria muralis)
ety: From Middle English penywort; equivalent to penny + wort.

senses: Something that is both a part and a whole.
ety: From holo- (from Ancient Greek ὅλος (hólos, “whole”)) + -on (like taxon or meron). Coined by Arthur Koestler in his 1967 book The Ghost in the Machine.

senses: Of an organism in which both copies of a given gene have the same allele
A flat tortilla that has been fried or toasted, or a dish based on this, usually associated with the cuisine of Latin America.
A bowl-shaped tortilla that has been fried and filled with various ingredients.
A Latin American toast (toasted bread).
ety: From Spanish tostada. Doublet of tostado.
examples: The Marina and Vicentino restaurants are good places for a coffee and tostada (toasted sandwich) for breakfast.
Tostada means any bread—tortillas or sliced loaves—that has been toasted. Any leftover bread or tostadas can be used in Torrijas (page 29) or ground into bread crumbs.

senses: A quick, energetic massage.
Synonym of dry transfer.
In Māori culture, an exchange of calls that forms part of the pōhiri.
examples: A karanga expert from within the manuhiri ope responds to the first karanga of the tangata whenua and indicates who they are.

senses: Being dried or withered.
A type of wetland in Patagonia.
examples: It is therefore not an uncommon sight to see the bones of cattle among the verdant green grasses of the mallins.
In the north they are called bajos and in the south mallins.
Other ecosystems at risk due to anthropogenic activities are the flood meadows so called "mallines". The mallines are wetlands in arid and semi-arid regions.

senses: That which drains.
A frame or rack for allowing washed crockery etc to dry naturally.
A perforated rack on which washed dishes, etc. may be placed in order to dry.
examples: The radical shift in mentality is even more necessary when analysts see Education simply as a drainer of resources.
I know that poor form is one of the biggest drainers of energy, so even though I slowed down significantly I made a very conscious effort to maintain good form.

senses: An elf; an inhabitant of fairy-land.
A little urchin or child.
ety: From Middle English elven, from Old English elfen, ælfen (“nymph, spirit, fairy”), feminine of elf, ælf (“elf”), equivalent to elf + -in. Cognate with Middle High German elbinne (“a fairy, nymph”).

senses: One who, or that which, prepares, fits, or makes ready.
An ancient drink resembling mead, made with mulberries.
A yellowish appearance in plants.
ety: From the Latin icterus, from the Ancient Greek ἴκτερος (íkteros, “jaundice”).

senses: The state or characteristic of drunkenness.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin inēbriātiō, inēbriātiōnem (“drunkenness”).

senses: A position in municipal governments in Spain and Latin America, roughly corresponding to alderman (member of municipal legislative body).
Written communications, especially in a business setting.
examples: I enjoy the newsgroup, the mailing lists, the email corro, and yakking on ICQ with these people.
As an aside, has anyone seen or heard from SAM? I want to get him some corro.
Hi Adrian, Some more corro around this matter. Can you advise when we'll get a brief?

senses: A style of parallel folding with the folds alternating between front and back; concertina fold.
Any printed material (book, leaflet etc.) having such folds; a concertina.
ety: Named after Leporello, the servant of the eponymous character in Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's opera Don Giovanni, who unfolds a long list of Don Giovanni's love conquests.
examples: Because of the accordion fold and leporello binding the book can be stretched out to its full length, showing a rich color field in transition.

senses: Someone who extorts; an extortioner.
Having or made of vertebrae.
Having a spinal column.
That lacks a thymus gland
A person who basks in the sun to get a tan.
examples: I went to the beach to look at the sunbathers, at least some of whom went there to be looked at while they worked on their tans.

senses: Without a car.
examples: Mr. Pence, the first sitting vice president to visit Mackinac Island, is apparently also the first government official to break with the island’s carless tradition.

senses: A coin issued by James III of Scotland; also a 15th-16th century Scottish coin worth four Scots pennies.
ety: From Middle Dutch placke (“name of a coin”). Cognate with Old High German pleh, bleh (“a thin leaf of metal, plate”). Compare plaque.

senses: The sound made by a hen, especially when brooding, or calling her chicks.
Any sound similar to this.
A kind of tongue click used to urge on a horse.
A setting hen.
ety: From Middle English clokken, clocken, from Old English cloccian (“to cluck, make a noise”), from Proto-West Germanic *klukkwōn, from Proto-Germanic *klukkwōną (“to make a sound, cluck”), of imitative origin. Cognate with Scots clok, clock (“to cluck”), Dutch klokken (“to cluck”), Low German klucken (“to cluck”), German glucken (“to cluck”), Danish klukke (“to cluck”), Swedish klucka (“to cluck”), Icelandic klökkva (“to sob, whine, cluck”).

senses: Lineage or genealogy, in Arab contexts.
Someone or something that squeezes.
A piece of foundry apparatus for shaping a ball of puddled iron.
A playing card that has its value shown in a corner such that a closely arranged hand may be studied (originally designed for poker but now standard).
Someone or something that coerces; one who puts the squeeze on someone.
examples: I made juice with a lemon squeezer.
Although it is possible to argue that the ogler's, pincher's, or squeezer's sexual misconduct is coercive, it is difficult.
Not all squeeze tactics rely on overt coercion, of course, as a squeezer's scheme sometimes can be achieved by lulling his squeezee into a false sense of security.

senses: Any squid-like cephalopods (marine mollusks) of the order Sepiida that have eight arms, two retractable tentacles, and a calcareous internal shell, and can eject a dark ink when threatened.
